idiom_name: reader/writer-locked unordered_map keyed to absolute steady_clock deadlines
implementation_notes: From C++17 the store is a std::unordered_map behind a std::shared_mutex: readers take a std::shared_lock and inspect an entry whose deadline is an absolute std::chrono::steady_clock time_point, and a miss is served by dropping the shared lock, loading from the source of truth and re-checking under a std::unique_lock before inserting, because a shared lock cannot be upgraded. std::optional distinguishes an absent entry from a cached empty value. Boost and oneTBB ship library caches when a hand-written table is unwanted; the std form is what the pattern looks like in modern C++.
pitfalls: std::shared_lock cannot be promoted to std::unique_lock: always re-check after taking the exclusive lock, or two threads populate the same key and the slower one wins.
Do not hold the mutex across the source-of-truth call unless serializing the miss path is intended - a blocking load inside the lock stalls every reader.
Use std::chrono::steady_clock for deadlines; system_clock jumps with NTP or manual time changes.

variants.name: std::mutex-guarded unordered_map (C++11 baseline)
variants.idiom_name: single-lock unordered_map with a monotonic deadline per entry
variants.implementation_notes: Before shared_mutex (C++17, with shared_timed_mutex available from C++14) the store is a std::unordered_map behind a plain std::mutex: every lookup takes the exclusive lock, so the critical section must stay tiny - find the entry, copy or move the value out, unlock, then do the source-of-truth read and the insert. Pick it for C++11 toolchains and small caches where a reader/writer lock would cost more than the contention it removes.
pitfalls: One mutex for the whole table serializes readers; keeping the source-of-truth I/O outside the lock is what stops the cache from being slower than the store under load.
emplace versus insert_or_assign decides whether a concurrently written entry survives - pick deliberately and re-check when it matters.
